full_judgment:
Syed Md. Ziaul Karim J: This Rule, at the instance of defendant-petitioner calls in question the legality and propriety of the order dated 13-6-2013 passed by learned Joint District Judge, first Court, Dhaka, rejecting an application for rejection of the plaint under Order VII, rule 11(d) and section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure (briefly as the Code) in Title Suit No. 462 of 2011.

2. Materials facts leading to this Rule are that on 25-5-2011 opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 462 of 2011 in the first Court of Joint District Judge, Dhaka, impleading the petitioner and opposite party Nos. 2-20 and others as defendants for the following relieves:

(ক) নালিশী ৩৩ শতাংশের কাতে ১৬১-১/২ শতাংশ ভূমির মালিক বাদিনী মর্মে স্বত্ব ঘোষণার ডিক্রি দিতে,

(খ) বাদিনীর বরাবর উক্ত ১৬১-১/২ শতাংশ ভূমির সাহাম বন্টনের নিমিত্তে ৰিবাদীগণের বিরুদ্ধে প্রাথমিক ডিক্রি দিতে

(গ) বিবাদীদের বিরুদ্ধে নালিশী ভূমির খাস দখল পুনরুদ্ধার সহ সার্ভে জানা এ্যাডভোকেট কমিশনার নিয়োগের মাধ্যমে সার্ভে করিয়া প্রদত্ত প্রতিবেদন অনুযায়ী নালিশী ১৬১-১/২ শতাংশ ভূমি চূড়ান্ত ডিক্রি দিতে,

(ঘ) ১নং বিবাদীর নামীয় জাল দলিল নং ১৩৫৯০ তাং ২৩-১২-৫৯ বাতিলের ডিক্রি দিতে,

(ঙ) মোকদ্দমার খরচ বাদিনীর অনুকূলে বিবাদীদের প্রতিকুলে ডিক্রি দিতে এবং

(চ) বাদিনী আইন ও ইক্যূইটি মতে আর যে যে প্রতিকার পাইতে তাহার ডিক্রি দিতে মর্জি হয় ৷

তপসিল

ঢাকা জেলার সাবেক কেরানীগঞ্জ হালে রমনা থানাধীন, ২৮০ এস, এ, ৬নং বড় মগবাজার মৌজান্থিত সি,এস, ৬২৮ পরে ১৮৭ এস, এ, ৫৮৬ নং খতিয়ানভুক্ত সি,এস, দাগ নং ৩৬৯ মোট ভূমি ১.১৮ ও ইহার কাতে ৮৩ শতাত্শ এবং এস, এ, ১০১ ৭ দাগের ৩২ শতাংশ ইহার কাতে ১৬-১/২ শতংশ ভূমি নালিশী ভূমি বটে ৷ ইহার আর, এস, খতিয়ান নং ১ ৭১ ৭, দাগ নং ৩৫৭৩ জমির পরিমাণ ২০৬৪ অযুতাংশ এবং আর, এস, খতিয়ান নং ১৫২২, দাগ নং ৩৬২০ জমির পরিমাণ, ১৩৮৮ মোট দুই দাগের কাতে, বাদিনীর, ১৬-১/২ শতাংশ নালিশী ভূমি বটে I যাহার চৌহদ্দি-উত্তরে রমজান আলি খান মজলিশ দক্ষিণে খোদা বক্স, পূর্বে আবদুল করিম, পশ্চিমে হামিদ হোসেন ৷

3. The petitioner as defendant No. 1 appeared in the suit by filing written statement denying all the materials allegations made in the plaint.

4. In suit, the defendant No. 1 by an application dated 10-1-2013 sought to reject the plaint of the suit under Order VII, rule 11(d) of the Code stating that suit is not maintainable in the present form; the suit is barred by res-judicata and by limitation inasmuch as identical relieves were sought by the plaintiff in previously instituted suit which was decided against him. So the instant suit is barred under law.

5. After hearing the learned Judge rejected the application by the impugned order holding that the question of res-judicata and limitation cannot be decided before trial.

6. Feeling aggrieved the petitioner preferred the instant Revision and obtained the present Rule.

7. The learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner seeks to impeach the impugned order on three fold arguments:

Firstly: That the instant suit the plaintiff claimed for declaration of title, recovery of possession partition and cancellation of the deed but those issues were earlier decided in Title Suit No. 164 of 1976 (re-number 239 of 1987 lastly renumbered as Title Suit No. 164 of 1997). So the instant suit is not at all maintainable.

Secondly: The instant suit is absolutely barred by limitation and res-judicata inasmiuchas the matter in issue directly and substantially in issue of the instant suit has been directly and substantially issue of the former suit, between the same parties.

Third and lastly: The learned Judge of the Court below failed to appreciate such question of law, thereby rejected the application for rejection of the plaint which is an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

8. In support of his contentions the learned Counsel refers the following cases:

(a) In the case of Abdul Jalil vs Islamic Bank Bangladesh Ltd. 53 DLR (AD) 12 held:

"Code of Civil Procedure : (V of 1908) Sections 11, 151 and Order VII, rule 11 It is well settled that where a plaint cannot be rejected under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure the court may invoke its inherent jurisdiction and reject the plaint taking recourse to section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

Sections 11, 151 and Order VII, rule 11

As the ultimate result of the suit is as clear as day light such a suit should be buried at its inception so that no further time is consumed in a fruitless litigation."

9. The learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1 opposes the Rule and submits that the relieves claimed in the instant suit are completely different from that of the former suit. So the plaint of the instant suit can-not be rejected before trial. He adds that the question of res-judicata is mixed question of fact and law which can be decided only at the trial on taking evidence. Moreso the plaintiff has an ample opportunity to amend her plaint at any time before trial. So the plaint cannot be rejected at this stage.

10. In support of his contentions he refers the following cases:

a) In the case of Sreemati Pushpa Rani Das vs AKM Habibur Rahman 13 BLD (AD) 217 held:

"Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

Order VII, rule 11.

The plea of res-judicata is not available in rejecting a plaint under Order VII, rule 11 CPC.-This matter can only be decided on the trial and it cannot be decided from a reading of the plaint res-judicata can be made an issue in the suit."

(b) In the case of Mahbubul Haque (Md.) vs Md. A Kader Munshi 52 DLR (AD) 49 = 20 BLD (AD) 82 held:

"Code of Civil Procedure (V of 1908)

Section-11

Rejection Order VII, rule 11(d)

Res-judicata of plaint—

Question res-judicata cannot be decided from a reading of the plaint and should be decided at the time of trial. Sreemati Pushpa Rani Das vs AKM Habibur Rahman, 13 BLD (AD) 217 relied.

Limitation

Question of limitation is a mixed question of law and fact which can be decided at the time of trial on taking evidence."

(c) In the case of Md. Shahabuddin vs Habibur Rahman 16 BLD (AD) 279 = 50 DLR (AD) 99 held: "Order VII, rule 11 Rejection of plaint on ground of limitation.

The question of limitation in a suit is a mixed question of law and fact which can be decided only in the trial on taking evidence. In view of the relieves prayed in the suit, the plaint cannot be rejected under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code."

11. In order to appreciate their submissions we have gone through the records and given our anxious considerations to their sub-missions.

12. The point for consideration whether the impugned order calls for interference by this Court.

13. For the convenience of understanding the provisions of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure reads hereunder:

"11—The plaint shall be rejected in the following issues: (a) Where it does not disclose a cause of action. (b) Where the relief claimed is under-valued, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to correct the valuation within a time to be fixed by the Court fails to do so; (c) Where the relief claimed is properly valued, but the plaint is written upon paper insufficiently stamped and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to supply the requisite stamp-paper within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails do so.(d) Where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law."

14. Provided that the time fixed by the Court for the correction of the valuation or sup-plying of the requisite stamp-paper shall not exceed twenty one days.

15. On going to the materials on record it transpires that earlier same plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 164 of 1976 (re-numbered as Title Suit No. 164 of 1997) for declaration of title in 0.161/2 acres of land appertaining to SA plot No. 1017, recovery of Khas possession in the suit property and for declaration that registered deed No. 13590 dated 23-12-1959 is fraud, fraudulent, inoperative and not binding upon him. The trial Court by its judgment and decree dated 28-2-2001 dismissed the suit holding:

“যেহেতু ১নং বিৰাদী ডি, ডব্লিউ-১ নিজেই স্বীকার করিয়াছেন যে, নালিশী এস, এ, ১০১৭ দাগের অর্ধেকাংশে বাদিনীয় স্বত্ব রহিয়াছে সেহেতু বাদিনীর স্বত্বের দাবীটি অবিশ্বাস করিৰার কোন কারণ নাই । তাহাছাড়া দালিলিক ভাবেও প্রমাণিত হইয়াছে যে, বাদিনী তাহার পূর্ববর্তী হামিদ হোসেনের নিকট হইতে খারিজ সূত্রে নালিশী দাগে l স্বত্ববান হইয়াছে ৷ বাদিনীর স্বত্বের আরো মজবুত ভিত্তি হইল তাহার বায়া হামিদ হোসেন নালিশী দাগে বাড়ী নির্মাণ করিয়া বসবাস করিতেছেন ৷ কিন্তু দুঃখজনকভাবে বাস্তবতা হইল বাদিনীর মোকদ্দমাটি যথাযথ আকারে দায়ের করা হয় নাই ৷ উভয় পক্ষের স্বীকৃত মতে এবং স্বীকৃত সি, এস, ১৮৭ খতিয়ান দৃষ্টে দেখা যায় সি,এস, ৩৬৯ দাগের মোট সম্পত্তি ১.১৮ একর ৷ কিন্তু আরজীর তপসিলে উক্ত দাগের ১৬-১/২ শতাংশ ভূমি বাবদ স্বত্ব সাব্যস্থ ক্রমে খাস দখলের প্রার্থনা করা হইঁয়াছে এবং উহাতে এস, এ, ১০১৭ দাগটি উল্লেখ করা হইয়াছে ৷ এস, এ, ১০১৭ দাগ সংক্রান্ত এস, এ, খতিয়ান ৫৮৬ পর্যালোচনা করিয়া দেখা যায় উহাতে ৩২ শতাংশ ভূমি হামিদ হোসেন এবং মোছাম্মৎ সৈয়দা সামসুজ্জাহান বেগমের নামে রেকর্ড হইয়াছে । অর্থাৎ না���িশী সম্পত্তি ভোগ, অনির্দিষ্ট এবং অচিহ্নিত ৷ যেহেতু সি,এস, খতিয়ান এবং দাগের ভূমি সম্পর্কে অদ্যাবধি বাই মিটস এন্ড রাউন্ড বিভাগ বন্টন হয় নাই সেহেতু বন্টনের মোকদ্দমা ব্যতীত বাদিনী কোন প্রকার প্রতিকার লাভ করিতে অধিকারী নহেন ৷ বণ্টনের মোকদ্দমা বাদিনী অবশ্যই প্রতিকার পাইতে অধিকারী হইবেন ৷ তবে স্বত্ব সাব্যস্ত ক্রমে খাস দখলের প্রার্থনায় আনীত মোকদ্দমাটিতে বাদিনী নালিশী সম্পত্তি তাহার দখল এবং বেদখলের ঘটনাটি প্রমাণ করিতে না পারার এবং নালিশী সম্পত্তি ভোগ, অনির্দিষ্ট ও অচিহ্নিত হওয়ায় বর্তমান আকারে ও প্ৰকারে মোকদ্দমাটি পরিচালনাযোগ্য নহে বর্তমান আকারে আনীত মোকদ্দমাটি তামাদিতে ও বারিত ৷ বাদীপক্ষ তাহার প্রার্থীত ক্রমে ডিক্রি কিংবা অন্য কোন প্রতিকার লাভ করিতে পারে না ৷ ১নং বিবাদিনীর নামীয় নালিশী ২৩-১ ২-৫৯ ইং তারিখের দলিলটি সম্পর্কে কোন প্রকার ঘোষণা লাভ করিতেও বাদীপক্ষ অধিকারী নহে ৷ মোকদ্দমাটি খারিজযোগ্য ৷”

16. Against the aforesaid judgment and decree the plaintiff preferred First Appeal No. 688 of 2001 before the High Court Division. After hearing the first appeal was dismissed by the judgment and decree dated 18-8-2009 holding:

"We are of the considered view that as the plaintiff appellant has got right, title in half portion of disputed SA plot No. 1017, she can get her share of land by filing a partition suit impleading all the co-sharers including defendant No. 1. From the evidence on record it appears that the plaintiff-appellant failed to prove her case of dispossession from the suit land and the present suit is not maintainable for non-specification of suit land and, as such, the learned Sub-ordinate Judge rightly dismissed the suit. We find no merit in the appeal.

In the result the appeal is dismissed without any order as to cost and the impugned order dated 28-2-2001 and decree dated 1-3-2001 are affirmed. The plaintiff-appellant is at liberty to file a fresh partition suit if she is so advised."

17. From the plain reading of the former suit it appears that the schedule given in that suit was unspecified. So in an unspecified land plaintiff is not entitled to get a decree. It is pertinent to point out that the High Court Division in its judgment held: that the plaintiff have got right, title in half portion of the disputed SA plot No. 1017, she got her share of land by filing a partition suit impleading all the co-sharers as defendants. Thereafter the plaintiff instituted the instant suit praying for the aforesaid relieves.

<u>18. The only point urged by the learned Counsel for the petitioner is that the instant suit is barred by res-judicata and also barred by limitation and the relieves claimed in the instant suit is substantially in issue in the former suit between the same parties. It has been well settled that the question of res-judicata and limitation raised in the application for rejecting the plaint are mixed question of law and fact which can only be decided at trial on taking evidence.</u>

19. In the case of Mahbubul Haque (Md.) vs Md. A Kader Munshi 52 DLR (AD) 49 held:

"Code of Civil Procedure (V of 1908)

Order VII, rule 11(d).

Question of limitation and res-judicata raised in the application for rejecting the plaint are mixed questions of law and fact which need thorough investigation on adequate evidence for arriving at a correct decision on framing specific issues by the trial Court."

20. The aforesaid views receives support in the case of Sreemati Pushpa Rani Das vs AKM Habibur Rahman 13 BLD (AD) 217 held:

"The plea of res-judicata is not available in rejecting a plaint under Order VII, rule 11 CPC.- This matter can only be decided on the trial and it cannot be decided from a reading of the plaint res-judicata can be made an issue in the suit."

21. And in the case of Shahabuddin vs Habibur Rahman 50 DLR (AD) 99=16 BLD (AD) 279, it was held that question of limitation is a mixed question of law and fact which can be decided at the time of trial on taking evidence.

<u>22. It further appears to us that in the former suit the trial Court as well as the Court of appeal categorically observed that the schedule of the plaint do not disclose any specification of the land in which the plaintiff sought for declaration of title. It is true that in an unspecified land no Court can grant any relief to the plaintiff. On careful scrutiny of the instant suit we find that the specification of the land has been clearly given in the instant suit. Moreso the plaintiff has an ample opportunity to amend the plaint in a justification form of relief, during pendency of the suit.</u>

23. In the case of Sk. Md. Junaid vs Turner Morrison and Co. Ltd. 26 DLR 111 held;

"Order VII, rule 11 (d) CPC.

Suit barred by limitation— It must prima facie appeared to be so-Court without rejecting the plaint, should allow it for amendment.

Clause (d) of rule 11, Order VII applies when it appears from the statements in the plaint that the suit is barred but it has no application when there is no clear or specific admission in the plaint suggesting that the suit is barred. This clause is attracted only when on the admitted facts as appearing from the plaint itself the suit is prima-facie barred. As for instance when from the statements made in the plaint it appears that the cause of action arose beyond the period of limitation fixed under the statute and no indication is given that limitation has been saved, the plaint may be rejected. In a proper case, when it appears to be barred by limitation, the plaint may be allowed to be amended without rejecting it. It is not mandatory for the Court to reject the plaint.

In the instant suit, it appears that the plaint was initially checked and sealed by the ministerial staff and then presented before the learned Sub-ordinate Judge. The Court then passed an order to register the plaint and issue notice upon the defendant, presumably on satisfaction that the plaint suffered from no latches with the meaning of Order VII, rule 11 CPC. In pursuance of the notices, the defendant-petitioner appeared and filed a petition praying for rejecting the plaint. The learned Judge in exercise of his discretion rejected the same without reasons recorded in the judgment. The original Court having disallowed the prayer for rejecting of the plaint by a judicial order, in exercise his discretion, we think, we should not interfere with the same under section 115 CPC and the lower Court passes a judicial order in exercise of its discretion, the High Court shall be reluctant to interfere with such order and there has been an absolute failure of justice of the case."

<u>24. Now coming to clause (d) of rule 11, it appears that clause (d) of the rule authorise the rejection of a plaint when the suit appears from the statements in the plaint to be barred by any law. This Clause applies when it appear from the statements in the plaint that the suit is barred but it has no application where there is no clear or specific admission in the plaint suggesting that the suit is barred. This clause is attracted only when on the admitted facts as appearing from the plaint itself the suit is prima facie barred. As for instance when from the statements made in the plaint it appears that the cause of action arose beyond the period of limitation fixed under the statute and no indication is given that limitation has been saved, the plaint may be rejected. In a proper case, when it appears to be barred by limitation, the plaint may be allowed to be amended without rejection. It is not mandatory for the Court to reject the pliant. It may ask the plaintiff to amend it so as to make suit maintainable. Where the plaintiff does not comply with such an order the Court may reject the plaint. Reference may be made to the cases reported in 18 CWN 1340. AIR 1928 Oudh 495 and AIR 1953 Cal 222.</u>

25. In the case of Ratan Chand Dharam Chand vs The Secretary of State for India in Council, reported in 18 CWN 1340, a Division Bench of Calcutta High Court while considering the scope of Order VII, rule 11(d) observed as follows :—

"That rule obviously has no application, for there was no statement in the plaint which suggested that the suit was barred. On the contrary it was specifically stated that notice under section 80 had been served on the "Collector" without specifying the district. The defect was not discovered till after the defendants had entered appearance and it was then too late to reject the plaint".

Similarly in the case of Maqsood Ali vs Deputy Commissioner, Bara Banki, reported in AIR 1928, Oudh, 495, a Division Bench of Oudh held that if the suit was not on the face of it barred by any law, Order VII, rule 11 (d) had no application. The relevant portion of the judgment ran as follows:

"We do not consider that the suit appeared from the statement in the plaint to be barred by law and we do not think that rule had any application. He has pointed out to us that in a suit which was filed in a similar manner a Bench of the Allahabad High Court stated in Nachhu vs Secy, of State that the plaint ought to have been rejected under the proviso of section 54(c) of the old Code of Civil Procedure, that clause was exactly the same as Order VII, rule 11 (d). The learned Judge composing the Bench gave no reasons for this conclusion and did not give any effect to it for we find that the suit with which they were concerned had been dismissed but the Sub-ordinate Judge and as their order was an order dismissing the appeal, the plaint was apparently not rejected. Their Lordships said: "It ought to have been rejected" but gave no effect to that view. We have only to note in respect of this point that exactly the same question could have been raised in Bhagchand Dagadusa vs Secy, of State. There the suit had been dismissed by the District Judge. The appeal had been dismissed by the High Court and the appeal was again dismissed by their Lordships of the Judicial Committee. It was not there suggested that the proper procedure was to reject the plaint. In a case such as this we are of opinion that the suit is not on the face of it barred by law. The very arguments which have been advanced in appeal show that the suit on the face of it is not barred by law, as the suit has been found to be a suit that has to be dismissed after consideration of the legal arguments. Therefore we are unable to accept this view of the learned Counsel.

26. The Calcata High Court in the case of Sreedam Chandra Bhur vs Tencori Mukherjee Reported in AIR 1959 Cal. 222 also held that Order VII, rule 11(d) was attracted only when on the admitted facts as papering from the plaint itself the suit was prima facie barred. The Division Bench in this connection observed as follows:-

"This clause is attracted only when on the admitted facts as appearing from the plaint itself the suit is prima facie barred. As for instance when from the statements made in the plaint it appears that the cause of action arose beyond period of limitation fixed under the statute and no indication is given that limitation has been saved, the plaint may be rejected. Even in such a case, an opportunity is to be given to the plaintiff to amend the plaint by setting out an acknowledgement in writing signed by the defendant within the period of limitation if it is so prayed, and that without passing an order for rejection of the plaint. 'Gunnaji Bhavaji vs Makanji Khoosal Chand', 34 Bom. 250. As was observed in 'Ratan Chand vs Secy, of State 18 Cal. WN 1340, action is to be taken under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of civil Procedure only if there is a clear and specific admission in the plaint from which it follows that the suit is barred. Reference may also be made to the observations of this Court.' Prankrishna vs Kripannath' 21 Cal WN 209 held:

"Let us now consider whether on the plaint as filed the Court will be justified in rejecting in limine the plaint under clause(d), rule 11, Order VII, Civil PC. In the body of the pliant there is no admission for the Council of the Assembly is the Government under section 80, Civil PC. On the other hand, it is seriously contested on behalf of the plaintiff that neither of the two bodies can even be deemed to be the government. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge refers to his order vaguely to the Trend of French Statutes conferring greater and  greater powers on the French Settlement in India and creating a 'Council du Government' there and later a cutting out Chandernagore from the Federation and conferring on Chandemagore all those powers with a separate delegate of the 'Commissionaire de la re-oblique, it is evident that the Chandernagore administration is a government in the grammatical and ordinary sense of the word though its functions may fall short of the those of the Governments existing in India.

We do not think it necessary to refer to other points urged before us by the con-tending parties. Suffice it to say that the question whether even if the Code of Civil Procedure applies, whether section 80 would be attracted or not cannot be decided merely on the plaint as it stands. The Court should have registered the plaint, issued notices on the defendants and allowed them to file their written statements. After issues were raised it would have been open to the Court to take up one or more of the issues as preliminary ones and decide the same. Objection that had been raised by the Court 'suo-motu' and such other objection as may be raised by the defendants would have to be tried on the merits, and only after all the necessary facts and materials are brought before the Court."

27. There is no reason to differ from the above principles of law. In the instant case, there is nothing on record to show that on the admitted facts as appearing from the plaint itself the suit is prima facie barred. So the rule 11 (d) is not at all attracted here and the plaint cannot be rejected on that score.

28. We find that both the parties are claiming their right, title, interest and possession in the suit land. So from the plain reading of the plaint of two suits we find that genealogy of acquiring title by the parties have been categorically described. Therefore we find that the grounds urged for rejection of the plaint are absolutely the subject-matter of evidence which cannot be decided before taking the evidence. On plain reading of the statements of the plaint it is evident that the same clearly discloses the cause of action the relieves claimed is not under valued, the plaint was not written upon paper insufficiently stamped and not barred by any other law.

29. In the case of Sundar Ali being dead his heirs: Mannan vs Md. Serajul Islam Sarker 56 DLR (AD) 210 held:

"For the ascertainment of the cause of action the Court is required to read the plaint in its entirety.

30. In the case of Abdul Malek Sawdagar vs Md. Mahbubey Alam 57 DLR (AD) 18 held:

"The question whether the plaint is liable to be rejected being barred by law must be apparent from the statement made in the plaint itself and not from the written statement or any other material other than that has been put in the plaint.

31. In the case of Md. Abul Khair vs Pubali Bank Ltd. 21 BLD (AD) 32 = 53 DLR (AD) 62 held:

Where in a suit an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code is filed for rejecting the plaint on the ground that the averments made in the plaint do no disclose a cause of action for the suit, the Court is not called upon to decide the suit on merit on taking evidence. It is only the averment made in the plaint which are to be considered to come to a finding as to whether those disclose a cause of action. The Court while deciding such application is not permitted in law to travel beyond the averments made in the plaint."

32. Therefore, the Court below after considering the materials on record and aforesaid principles of law, by rejecting the application committed no error of law. Moreso, it appears that findings arrived at by the Court below having been rested upon consideration and discussions of materials on record and also on a correct and proper analysis of legal aspects involved in suit. Moreover, we do not find any misreading or misappreciation of the materials on record. Therefore, the findings of the Court below are not liable to be disturbed by the High Court Division in exercise of power under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

33. Moreover the impugned order in its entirety is well founded in the facts and circumstances of the case. So, the submissions advanced by the learned Counsel for the petitioner are not the correct exposition of law and facts. However we have gone through the decisions as referred by him. We are in respectful agreement with the principles enunciated therein but the facts leading to those cases are quite distinguishable to that of the instant case. Therefore we are unable to accept his submissions. On the contrary the submissions advanced by the learned Counsel for the opposite party No. 1 prevail and appear to have a deal of force.

34. In the light of discussions made above and the preponderant judicial views emerging out of the authorities referred to above, we are of the view that the impugned order suffers from no legal infirmity which calls for no interference by this. Court. Thus the Rule having no merit fails.

35. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost. The order of stay granted earlier stands vacated.

The office is directed to communicate the order at once.

End.
